Yellowstone's climate is greatly influenced by altitude, with lower elevations generally found to be warmer year-round. The record high temperature was 99 °F (37 °C) in 2002, while the coldest temperature recorded is −66 °F (−54 °C) in 1933.[[11]](#cite_note-facts-11) During the summer months of June to early September, daytime highs are normally in the 70 to 80 °F (21 to 27 °C) range, while nighttime lows can go to below freezing (0 °C), especially at higher altitudes. Summer afternoons are frequently accompanied by [thunderstorms](/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm"). Spring and fall temperatures range between 30 and 60 °F (−1 and 16 °C) with nights in the teens to single digits (−5 to −20 °C). Winter in Yellowstone is accompanied by high temperatures usually between 0 and 20 °F (−18 and −7 °C) and nighttime temperatures below 0 °F (−18 °C) for most of the winter.[[145]](#cite_note-weather-148)

Precipitation in Yellowstone is highly variable and ranges from 15 inches (380 mm) annually near Mammoth Hot Springs to 80 inches (2,000 mm) in the southwestern sections of the park. The precipitation of Yellowstone is greatly influenced by the moisture channel formed by the [Snake River Plain](/wiki/Snake_River_Plain "Snake River Plain") to the west that was, in turn, formed by Yellowstone itself. Hawaii :: Etymology :: chunk_0007
The State of Hawaii derives its name from the name of its largest island, [Hawaiʻi](/wiki/Hawaii_(island) "Hawaii (island)"). A common explanation of the name of Hawaiʻi is that it was named for [Hawaiʻiloa](/wiki/Hawaiiloa "Hawaiiloa"), a figure from Hawaiian oral tradition. He is said to have discovered the islands when they were first settled.[[22]](#cite_note-27)[[23]](#cite_note-28)

The [Hawaiian language](/wiki/Hawaiian_language "Hawaiian language") word *Hawaiʻi* is very similar to [Proto-Polynesian](/wiki/Proto-Polynesian_language "Proto-Polynesian language") *\*Sawaiki*, with the [reconstructed](/wiki/Internal_reconstruction "Internal reconstruction") meaning 'homeland'.[[f]](#cite_note-29) [Cognates](/wiki/Cognate "Cognate") of *Hawaiʻi* are found in other Polynesian languages, including [Māori](/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language") (*[Hawaiki](/wiki/Hawaiki "Hawaiki")*), [Rarotongan](/wiki/Cook_Islands_Maori "Cook Islands Maori") (*ʻAvaiki*) and [Samoan](/wiki/Samoan_language "Samoan language") (*[Savaiʻi](/wiki/Savai%27i "Savai'i")*). According to linguists Pukui and Elbert,[[24]](#cite_note-30) "elsewhere in Polynesia, *Hawaiʻi* or a cognate is the name of the underworld or of the ancestral home, but in Hawaii, the name has no meaning".[[25]](#cite_note-31)

Ben Bernanke :: Nobel Prize :: chunk_0015
In 2022 Bernanke was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences along with [Philip H. Dybvig](/wiki/Philip_H._Dybvig "Philip H. Dybvig") and [Douglas Diamond](/wiki/Douglas_Diamond "Douglas Diamond"). Their research suggested that the Great Depression was caused by a variety of factors including credit market stress and a failing gold standard. With a rising [External Finance Premium](/w/index.php?title=External_Finance_Premium&action=edit&redlink=1 "External Finance Premium (page does not exist)") lenders and borrowers were both inclined to protect their financial health due to stressed credit markets. Lenders began tightening credit standards and avoiding risky borrowers while borrowers withdrew their cash. These self-preservation decisions from both lenders and borrowers resulted in further stress on the credit market and stagnation in investment spending. In addition to stressed credit markets, the failing gold standard also played a crucial role. After World War 1 most countries had their currencies tied to gold as well as fixed exchange rates, however, post-war animosity between many European nations led to non-cooperation regarding the gold standard. Consequently, the gold standard failed in the late 1920s, bringing prices, money supply, and output down with it. Their research showed that the combination of a failing gold standard and stressed credit markets led to a catastrophic spiral in the economy.[[91]](#cite_note-91)
